title: Security review - Audit logs (schema, exports, retention)
next_steps: Redwood to send audit event schema v1 excerpt + example events (API key rotation, RBAC role update, model rollout).
Redwood to confirm current retention options (hosted vs dedicated vs private) and planned retention controls for GA.

transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Security review - Audit logs (schema, exports, retention)
Date: 2025-06-12
Start time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 52 min

Attendees:
- Redwood Inference: Rachel Kim, Marcus Lin, Olga Petrov, Liam O'Rourke
- HelioBank: Priya Desai, Jon Marshall, Elena Varga, Samir Khan

---
Auto Summary (generated)
- HelioBank requested detailed confirmation of audit log coverage for security-sensitive actions (RBAC/auth changes, API keys, deployments/rollouts, capacity changes) and asked how Redwood guarantees completeness.
- Redwood walked through the canonical audit event schema v1 approach (versioning, required fields, actor/target modeling, request correlation, outcome/error semantics) and how events are validated.
- Export options discussed: S3 (JSONL), webhook, and Splunk-style integrations; HelioBank emphasized SIEM reliability, backpressure, and replay.
- Retention and redaction: HelioBank asked about IP/user-agent retention and ability to control retention for privacy; Redwood described configurable retention tiers and redaction rules to prevent secret leakage.

Topics
1) What is logged (sensitive actions) and “coverage” definition
2) Schema stability + versioning strategy
3) Export formats, sinks (S3/SIEM), failure handling
4) Retention, redaction, and internal access controls
5) Private deployment considerations

Questions captured
- Do you guarantee 100% logging for sensitive actions, and how do you prevent “silent gaps”?
- Is the audit schema versioned and backward compatible? What constitutes a breaking change?
- Can we export to S3 and Splunk, and do we get delivery metrics / retry behavior?
- What’s your retention default and can we set it to 1 year+? Can we disable IP/user-agent if needed?
- Do you audit access to the audit logs themselves (admin reads/exports)?

Action items
- Rachel Kim - Send HelioBank the current audit logs FAQ / PRD excerpt and confirm planned GA dates for export sinks - Due 2025-06-13
- Marcus Lin - Provide a short written statement on schema versioning + breaking change policy and any signing/immutability controls - Due 2025-06-16
- Olga Petrov - Map HelioBank’s SOC 2 evidence asks to Redwood audit logging controls (field-level mapping + sample export) - Due 2025-06-18
- Liam O'Rourke - Set up a technical deep dive with SREs on delivery lag SLO + exporter retry/backoff and replay strategy - Due 2025-06-17

---
Transcript

[00:00] Rachel Kim: Alright, we’re at the top of the hour. Thanks everyone for joining. This is Rachel from Redwood. The agenda today is audit logs—what we log, the schema, retention, and export. I’ve got Marcus from Security Engineering, Olga from GRC, and Liam who’s our TAM on the evaluation.

[00:18] Priya Desai: Great, thanks Rachel. Yeah, we’re mostly trying to close out a security questionnaire section. Audit logging is kind of the gating item for us.

[00:28] Jon Marshall: And I’ll just add we’re evaluating both hosted and potentially dedicated later. Private maybe down the road, but we want to understand the consistency.

[00:38] Rachel Kim: Perfect. Maybe quick intros and then we’ll jump in. Marcus?

[00:43] Marcus Lin: Hey all, Marcus Lin. I run Security Engineering at Redwood. I’m close to the audit logging program, schema standardization work, and how we enforce coverage across services.

[00:54] Olga Petrov: Hi, Olga Petrov, GRC Director. I help align what we build with SOC 2 and ISO evidence expectations.

[01:02] Liam O'Rourke: Liam O’Rourke here, TAM. I’ll help answer operational questions—exports, SLOs, and what you can expect day to day.

[01:10] Priya Desai: Great. I’m Priya, security architect. Elena is here from compliance.

[01:14] Elena Varga: Hi.

[01:16] Samir Khan: Samir, SRE. I’ll probably ask annoying reliability questions.

[01:20] Rachel Kim: Those are the good questions.

[01:23] Priya Desai: Okay, so starting point—when we say audit logs, we need to see admin activity, auth changes, keys, and also anything that affects availability or routing. Can you confirm the scope?

[01:39] Marcus Lin: Yep. Our definition of “sensitive actions” is: any action that materially affects customer data access, security posture, billing, or availability. Concretely that means RBAC changes, user/admin management, API key creation/rotation/revocation, org/workspace settings, model deployment and rollout actions, routing/fallback policy changes, dedicated capacity scaling and quota changes, private install/upgrade/rollback, data retention configuration changes, and audit log configuration changes.

[02:07] Priya Desai: Good. And are those all consistently logged today?

[02:12] Marcus Lin: Some are live, some are in flight as part of a standardization effort. The program goal is 100% coverage for those sensitive actions, and we’re enforcing it via a canonical schema, a shared library, and a coverage inventory with CI checks. So rather than “we think we log it,” we’re making it mechanically difficult to ship a sensitive action without an audit event.

[02:37] Jon Marshall: Can you define “100% coverage” precisely? Because vendors sometimes mean “best effort.”

[02:44] Marcus Lin: Totally fair. For us it means: for each sensitive action in the inventory, there’s at least one expected audit event name. And for each event, we validate it contains the required fields and is delivered to the audit log pipeline. We also have integration tests that perform the action in staging and assert the event exists with the required envelope—request id, actor, target, outcome, timestamp, org scope, and so on.

[03:12] Samir Khan: So it’s like an allowlist? If a new sensitive action is introduced it has to be registered?

[03:18] Marcus Lin: Exactly. Event names are registered. If a team adds a new sensitive action, they must update the inventory and ensure the event is emitted. We’re adding a build-time check that blocks unregistered event names, and separately a coverage scanner that compares the inventory to emitted/validated events.

[03:40] Priya Desai: Okay. I want to dig into schema. We’ve been burned by logs changing format.

[03:47] Marcus Lin: Schema stability is a core design point. We have a canonical “audit event schema v1.” It’s versioned, and we treat backward compatibility seriously. Practically: we can add optional fields at any time. We do not rename required fields or change their meaning without a new major version. Event names are also designed to be stable—verb.resource style, namespaced.

[04:10] Elena Varga: When you say versioned, do you include a field in each record? Like “schema_version”?

[04:16] Marcus Lin: Yes—each record includes a schema version, and the event name itself is separate from version. So you’ll see something like “schema_version: 1.0” plus an “event_name” like “rbac.role.updated” or “api_key.rotated.”

[04:33] Jon Marshall: Do you have a JSON schema we can validate against on our side?

[04:38] Marcus Lin: We do. Internally we use JSONSchema for validation; for customers we can provide the schema and a changelog. If you ingest via S3 you can enforce it in your pipeline too.

[04:52] Priya Desai: Required fields—what’s in the envelope?

[04:55] Marcus Lin: High level required fields: event_name, event_id, timestamp, schema_version, org identifiers (org_id, workspace_id where applicable), actor (who did it), target (what was acted on), request correlation (request_id, trace_id when present), source (service name, environment, region), network context (ip, user_agent if present), and outcome semantics—success/failure with error codes.

[05:25] Samir Khan: “If present” worries me. Is IP always there?

[05:29] Marcus Lin: Good nuance. For UI and API gateway initiated actions, we generally have IP and user-agent. For internal controllers—like a rollout controller initiating a canary toggle—there may not be a user-agent, and IP may be service-to-service. In those cases, we still populate actor as a service identity and preserve request_id/trace_id where we can, but we’re careful not to fabricate user context.

[05:56] Priya Desai: Actor attribution is a big one. If an automated process changes routing policy, we need to know it wasn’t a human.

[06:05] Marcus Lin: Right. Our actor model distinguishes between user actors and service actors. So you’ll see actor.type = “user” with user_id/email for console actions, or actor.type = “service” with service name and credential identity for automated actions. And there’s also an “initiator” concept when something is triggered by a user but executed by a controller—like user clicks “start canary,” controller does the work; we record both.

[06:33] Jon Marshall: Can you include the “diff” for RBAC changes? Like what permissions changed?

[06:38] Marcus Lin: Yes. For RBAC policy updates we include a before/after diff payload. We do redaction on anything that looks like a secret, token, or credential. For RBAC diffs it’s usually safe, but we still scrub dangerous keys by rule.

[06:56] Elena Varga: We also need to show auditors that audit logs are protected. Can you speak to tamper resistance?

[07:03] Marcus Lin: Sure. At a platform level we treat the pipeline as append-only. Access to raw logs is restricted internally. We’re also exploring signing for export artifacts, but today the primary controls are: restricted write path, append-only storage semantics, immutability controls on the storage layer, and monitoring for anomalies. Olga can map that to SOC 2 controls.

[07:27] Olga Petrov: Yeah, from evidence perspective, auditors want to see that logs are generated, protected from alteration, and reviewable. We can provide our access policy, and we can show that internal access to audit logs is itself logged.

[07:41] Priya Desai: Wait—you log internal access to customer audit logs?

[07:45] Olga Petrov: Yes, internal queries to raw audit logs require approval and are audited. For the customer-facing product, “reading the audit logs” via the console Audit Logs page is also an auditable action for admin users.

[08:00] Samir Khan: That’s good. On reliability: what’s the delivery lag expectation? Like if I rotate a key, when does the event appear in export?

[08:09] Liam O'Rourke: Today our target is near-real-time, but we measure it explicitly as delivery lag—time from event emission to persistence and export. We’re implementing an SLO with alerting. For most actions you should see it within a few minutes; we can share the SLO target and historical baseline once we enable it for your env.

[08:33] Samir Khan: “Few minutes” might be fine, but we need to know if things can drop.

[08:37] Liam O'Rourke: The design goal is no silent drops. We treat export as at-least-once delivery with retries and dead-letter behavior when a sink is down. That means you may see duplicates in some failure modes, and we recommend de-duping by event_id on your side.

[08:58] Jon Marshall: So exports are at-least-once. What sinks do you support today?

[09:03] Liam O'Rourke: Common ones are S3 as JSON lines (one event per line), webhook delivery, and SIEM integrations. For Splunk specifically, we typically support an HTTP Event Collector style push; if you’re using something else we can align.

[09:21] Priya Desai: We primarily use Splunk and also archive to S3 for cold storage.

[09:27] Rachel Kim: That matches what we see with other banks. We can support S3 and Splunk-style. Part of the enterprise packaging discussion is exactly these sink options.

[09:38] Elena Varga: On retention: what’s default and what’s configurable?

[09:42] Rachel Kim: High level: we have a default retention window in the product, and for enterprise we offer extended retention tiers. We’re also building controls around retention configuration and ensuring changes to retention are audited.

[09:56] Priya Desai: Can we get to 365 days retention? That’s our baseline.

[10:00] Rachel Kim: In enterprise plans, yes, that’s the target. There are some nuances in private deployments depending on customer-managed storage, but we can support one year retention.

[10:13] Jon Marshall: For private, do you run the same exporter stack?

[10:17] Liam O'Rourke: Private deployments use the same logical pipeline—ingest, validate, store, export—but the control plane and storage can be in your environment depending on the setup. The installer and upgrade actions themselves are auditable events as well.

[10:34] Samir Khan: For private, if we have a network outage to Splunk, will it queue locally? Or does it just fail?

[10:41] Liam O'Rourke: It queues and retries with backoff. There’s also a dead-letter queue mechanism so you can inspect failures. And we expose metrics: enqueue rate, persist success, export success, export failures by sink.

[11:00] Priya Desai: Do we get those metrics?

[11:02] Liam O'Rourke: In product you’ll see exporter health and delivery lag dashboards. In private you can also scrape metrics in your monitoring stack.

[11:12] Priya Desai: Okay. Now content. We specifically need: API key rotation, API key revoke, RBAC role change, user added/removed, and model deployment changes. Do you have named events for those?

[11:29] Marcus Lin: Yes. API key create/revoke/rotate are separate event names. RBAC has role created/updated/deleted and permission bundle updated, including diffs. User admin actions are logged. Model deployment actions include deploy, rollback, canary start/stop, pin/unpin versions, and fallback policy changes.

[11:56] Jon Marshall: What about “read access”—like someone viewing prompts or logs. Do you log data reads?

[12:02] Marcus Lin: We log administrative access to sensitive settings and audit logs. For application-level reads—like a user calling inference APIs—that’s typically not an audit log event; that’s an access log / usage log stream. For audit logs we focus on control-plane sensitive actions. If your requirement is “who read what record,” that’s a different feature set and usually not feasible for inference payloads due to volume and privacy.

[12:30] Priya Desai: That’s fine, we mainly care about admin actions and changes.

[12:35] Elena Varga: Data privacy: IP address and user-agent—are those always included? We have some regional constraints.

[12:43] Marcus Lin: For hosted, we capture IP and user-agent for requests through the gateway. For privacy, we have redaction rules—no secrets, no tokens, no full API keys. For IP/user-agent, the approach we’re taking is: make it available as default for security value, and provide documented retention guidance and, in some cases, configuration to minimize or hash certain fields. We need to align on exact options based on your legal requirements.

[13:14] Priya Desai: We might need the option to suppress user-agent. IP we usually keep.

[13:20] Marcus Lin: Understood. We can follow up with specifics on what’s configurable at GA versus what’s policy-controlled.

[13:29] Samir Khan: Another reliability question: how do you correlate audit logs with a request? Like I want to tie a key rotation to the admin request in the console.

[13:38] Marcus Lin: We propagate request_id end-to-end. For console, there’s a request id from the frontend through the backend; for API it’s the gateway request id. We also can attach trace_id if you’re using distributed tracing hooks. So audit event includes request_id, and you can match it to other logs.

[13:58] Jon Marshall: Schema stability—do you ever change event names?

[14:02] Marcus Lin: We avoid it. If we must, we dual-write for a deprecation window: emit both old and new event names, document the mapping, and then cut over. That’s explicitly part of our migration plan from legacy event names.

[14:20] Priya Desai: What’s the deprecation window? 30 days? 90 days?

[14:24] Marcus Lin: Typically 90 days for enterprise customers, longer if contractually required. We’d communicate it clearly.

[14:33] Elena Varga: Do you have a change log?

[14:35] Marcus Lin: Yes. We maintain a schema changelog and we can notify via release notes. Also, export artifacts can include schema_version so your pipeline can branch.

[14:49] Rachel Kim: Priya, can I ask—what does your security review require as proof? Is it enough to see sample events and documentation, or do you need to test export into Splunk before procurement?

[15:00] Priya Desai: We need both. Documentation for the questionnaire and a quick validation during pilot that events show up in Splunk within a reasonable time.

[15:11] Liam O'Rourke: That’s doable. We can set up a pilot sink to Splunk HEC or to S3 and then you forward.

[15:18] Samir Khan: Prefer direct HEC, less moving parts.

[15:21] Liam O'Rourke: Got it.

[15:24] Jon Marshall: Can you talk about how you prevent developers from accidentally logging secrets into audit logs? Like if someone includes an API key value in the payload.

[15:34] Marcus Lin: Two layers. First, the shared library provides structured fields and discourages free-form payloads. Second, we run redaction rules on payloads in the pipeline and in some client libraries—scrub known sensitive keys, patterns, and token-like strings. We also test redaction, and we have a policy that audit events must never include raw credentials.

[15:59] Priya Desai: Okay. And do you include “before/after” for capacity changes?

[16:03] Marcus Lin: Yes. For dedicated scaling, we include before and after desired capacity, and whether it was manual or autoscaling.

[16:11] Samir Khan: Is autoscaling considered a sensitive action? It’s automated.

[16:14] Marcus Lin: It can impact availability and cost, so yes; we log it with actor.type = service and include the policy source.

[16:25] Elena Varga: For SOC 2, we need to show log retention is enforced. Is retention change itself logged?

[16:33] Marcus Lin: Yes, retention config changes are sensitive actions and audited.

[16:39] Olga Petrov: Also we can provide control mapping: which events and fields correspond to change management and access controls. Auditors typically ask “show me evidence of reviewable logs and that changes are tracked.”

[16:55] Priya Desai: We may ask for an auditor-friendly export. Like a CSV.

[16:59] Rachel Kim: The export format is generally JSON for fidelity, but the UI can export CSV for convenience. For SIEM integrations, JSON is the standard.

[17:10] Jon Marshall: How about filtering? We don’t want everything, just the sensitive events.

[17:14] Liam O'Rourke: The product is audit logs only, so it’s already filtered to that class. Within that, you can filter by event_name, actor, target, time window, outcome, and so on.

[17:27] Samir Khan: Rate limiting—if we query the Audit Logs API, is it limited?

[17:31] Liam O'Rourke: Yes, admin APIs are rate limited to protect the service, but exports are designed for bulk delivery. We can size it to your needs.

[17:43] Priya Desai: How do you handle multi-region? If we’re in EU region and US region.

[17:48] Liam O'Rourke: Audit logs are generated in-region and stored per region consistent with the deployment. For export, you can configure sinks per region. We can also discuss residency requirements.

[18:03] Jon Marshall: Okay. I want to ask the uncomfortable question: how do you prove completeness? Like, if an event fails validation, what happens? Does it get dropped?

[18:13] Marcus Lin: If an event fails schema validation, it is treated as an error; we don’t silently drop. We alert, and the emitting service can fail the request or degrade depending on the action. For sensitive actions, our policy is: prefer failing the operation over proceeding without an audit event, unless there’s a documented exception approved by Security.

[18:38] Priya Desai: That’s actually what we want.

[18:41] Samir Khan: But that can create availability risk, right? If audit pipeline is down you can’t rotate keys.

[18:47] Marcus Lin: Correct, it’s a tradeoff. For truly critical safety actions we’d rather block than lose auditability. For some actions we may allow local buffering and eventual delivery, but again not silent. We can walk through which actions are “must-audit” hard dependencies.

[19:11] Jon Marshall: So there’s an exception process.

[19:14] Marcus Lin: Yes, documented exceptions with time bounds.

[19:18] Elena Varga: Do you have a policy document you can share?

[19:21] Olga Petrov: We can share an overview and the relevant policy excerpts under NDA. It covers internal access and how exceptions are handled.

[19:33] Priya Desai: One more: do you log “export configuration changes” like adding a new webhook destination?

[19:40] Marcus Lin: Yes. Audit log configuration changes are explicitly in-scope. So creating/modifying an export sink is a sensitive action and produces an event.

[19:52] Samir Khan: Webhooks—do you sign webhook payloads?

[19:56] Liam O'Rourke: We support shared-secret signing for webhooks. For S3, integrity is handled via bucket policies and optional object lock depending on your setup. If you need cryptographic signing of every event, that’s something we can discuss; it’s not always required, but some regulated customers ask.

[20:22] Priya Desai: We may not need per-event signing if the storage is immutable. We mostly need strong access control and evidence.

[20:31] Rachel Kim: Makes sense.

[20:34] Jon Marshall: Can we see example events? Specifically API key rotation and RBAC change.

[20:39] Marcus Lin: Yes, we can send redacted samples after the call. They’ll show actor, target, outcome, request_id, and diff payload for RBAC.

[20:52] Elena Varga: Also retention—if we export to S3, can we keep indefinitely even if Redwood retention is shorter?

[21:00] Liam O'Rourke: Yes. Your export sink becomes your system of record. Redwood’s in-product retention governs what’s queryable in the console/API, but export can be continuous and you can store as long as you want.

[21:15] Samir Khan: As long as export is reliable.

[21:17] Liam O'Rourke: Exactly why we’re focusing on exporter reliability, backpressure, and metrics.

[21:24] Priya Desai: Do you provide a delivery report? Like “events exported” vs “events generated.”

[21:30] Liam O'Rourke: We provide metrics: number enqueued, persisted, exported, failures, and lag distribution. And we can expose a “drop rate” concept—ideally zero—versus delay. If something is stuck in DLQ, that’s visible.

[21:54] Jon Marshall: What about “billing” actions? Like quota changes.

[21:57] Marcus Lin: Those are also in scope. Quota changes, plan changes, anything that affects billing or usage limits is audited.

[22:09] Priya Desai: Okay. I think that covers most. Elena, any compliance-specific gaps?

[22:15] Elena Varga: Just evidence. Olga, you said you can map to SOC 2—can you send that mapping? Even a high-level.

[22:22] Olga Petrov: Yes. We’ll send a high-level control mapping and a description of how to pull audit exports and what fields are relevant.

[22:32] Rachel Kim: Samir, anything else from SRE side?

[22:35] Samir Khan: Maybe one: if Splunk is down for, say, 6 hours, how big is the buffer? And do you replay automatically?

[22:44] Liam O'Rourke: Buffering depends on the deployment and configuration; we size the queue and can scale consumers. Replay is automatic via retries; if it exceeds a threshold it moves to DLQ and keeps retry metadata. In a prolonged outage, we’ll alert and you can either fix the sink and let it drain or reroute to S3 temporarily.

[23:09] Samir Khan: Okay, as long as there’s a runbook.

[23:12] Liam O'Rourke: There is, and we can share an excerpt.

[23:16] Priya Desai: Timeline—when is this “schema v1 + coverage enforcement” considered GA?

[23:23] Rachel Kim: We’re in the final stretch of standardization now. For your pilot, we can enable the audit logs export and confirm the set of sensitive events you listed. The broader GA includes the dashboards, CI enforcement, and exporter hardening. I’ll send the latest target dates after checking with the team.

[23:46] Jon Marshall: Alright.

[23:48] Priya Desai: This has been helpful. If you send schema, samples, and retention options in writing, we can close the questionnaire.

[23:58] Rachel Kim: Great. Let’s do a quick recap of next steps.

[24:02] Rachel Kim: One—Marcus will send a schema v1 overview and sample events for API key rotation and RBAC changes. Two—Olga will send a SOC2 evidence/control mapping excerpt. Three—Liam will set up a technical deep dive with Samir on export reliability and delivery lag SLOs, and we’ll align on Splunk HEC details.

[24:24] Samir Khan: Works.

[24:25] Priya Desai: Yep.

[24:27] Rachel Kim: Anything else before we drop?

[24:30] Jon Marshall: No, thanks.

[24:32] Rachel Kim: Alright, thanks everyone.

[Recording ends early in transcript due to partial capture; remaining discussion continued off-record for ~25 minutes focused on Splunk endpoint details and NDA doc sharing.]
